## Conference overview

*Preview by Wes Reynolds, p. 149. Reproduced in full.*


> The Big Ten is aiming for its fourth consecutive CFP National Championship here in 2026.

> In 2023, Michigan won its first national title since 1997 before Jim Harbaugh left his alma mater and took his NCAA show-cause penalty to return to coaching in the NFL.

> In 2024, the Wolverines’ archrival Ohio State, led by the most talented roster in college football, removed the critics from Ryan Day’s back and won its first national title since 2014.

> Well, the Big Ten “three-peated” last season.

> So, was it Ohio State again?

> No, it was the Indiana Hoosiers going 16-0 and becoming the first FBS team since Yale in 1894 to go 16-0.

> Curt Cignetti and his Hoosiers also won their first outright Big Ten Championship since 1945.

> Indiana’s rise to national prominence not only included these championships but was also home to its first Heisman Trophy Winner Fernando Mendoza.

> Indiana (+250) will attempt to defend with heavy retention on the offensive line and defense to go along with a portal overhaul that includes TCU transfer QB Josh Hoover to replace Mendoza.

> Ohio State (+180), defeated by the Hoosiers in the Big Ten Championship Game, returns QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith as perhaps the best QB-WR tandem in college football.

> Oregon (+260), who lost to the Hoosiers twice, brings back 14 starters including QB Dante Moore and arguably the nation’s best defensive line.

> Those three teams will be consensus top five nationally to start the season, but USC (14-1) is looking to get to the top of the Big Ten for the first time with a defense led by former TCU coach Gary Patterson, who was lured out of retirement.

> Four programs have new coaches including Michigan (15-1), who brings in Kyle Whittingham from Utah to restore its tarnished image from the Harbaugh recruiting violations and the Sherrone Moore scandal; Michigan State (500-1), who turns to former Northwestern head coach Pat Fitzgerald; Penn State (20-1), who brings in Matt Campbell from Iowa State to win the big ones that James Franklin seemingly never could; UCLA (160-1), who figured that if Indiana can hire a successful head coach from James Madison, then why not do the same with Bob Chesney? big TEN

- **Indiana Hoosiers** (p. 152) — Cignetti kept his staff intact plus returns 10 starters (six on defense for Broyles Award winning defensive coordinator Bryant Haines) and adds eight other Power Four starters by way of the portal, including TCU QB Josh Hoover, the current active FBS passing leader with 9,629 yards and 71 touchdowns in 36 games (31 starts), who will start behind arguably the best offensive line in college football.

- **Michigan State Spartans** (p. 160) — While there are certainly plenty of roster questions across the board, Sparty must feel as good about its QB situation as they have in the last few seasons.

- **Michigan Wolverines** (p. 159) — On the surface, he should be improved just with better coaching and development under new offensive coordinator Jason Beck and QB coach Koy Detmer.

- **Minnesota Golden Gophers** (p. 162) — Minnesota returns 68% of its 2025 production per ESPN’s Bill Connelly and is led by redshirt sophomore quarterback Drake Lindsey (63.5%, 2432 yards, 19/6 TD/INT), who started all 13 games as a freshman.

- **Nebraska Cornhuskers** (p. 164) — Dylan Raiola, a legacy player whose father Dominic and uncle Donovan played at Nebraska, was thought to be the savior at quarterback for which Nebraska has been searching.

## Schedule themes


**From the conference preview (p. 149):**

> Indiana’s rise to national prominence not only included these championships but was also home to its first Heisman Trophy Winner Fernando Mendoza.
>
> — *conference preview, p. 149*


**From the team pages in this conference** — 16 of 18 teams' pages address this theme. A sample follows; Phase 3 carries the full treatment team by team.


- **Illinois Fighting Illini** (p. 150) — The schedule is manageable and the Illini should start with three non-conference victories playing UAB, Duke, and Southern Illinois at home.

- **Indiana Hoosiers** (p. 152) — 10.5 is the right number for Indiana’s win total when you look at another manageable schedule where the Hoosiers avoid a double revenge spot with Oregon (perhaps until the Big 10 Championship Game) and will be favored in every game apart from Ohio State (small home dog).

- **Iowa Hawkeyes** (p. 154) — The schedule begins with three non-conference home games, but two of them are against in-state rivals Iowa State and Northern Iowa.

- **Maryland Terrapins** (p. 156) — Locksley has always been a high-level recruiter, and he has brought big-time talent into the program and has kept DMV talent from leaving home, but he cannot live off the 23-16 three-season run (2021-2023) forever.

- **Michigan Wolverines** (p. 158) — On the other hand, he and his Wolverines get a “welcome to the Big Ten” schedule that has six ranked opponents on it and does not get to avoid any of the top teams in conference play.

- **Minnesota Golden Gophers** (p. 162) — The Gophers get a break in the schedule avoiding Ohio State and Oregon but still must travel to Indiana, Penn State, and Washington.

- **Nebraska Cornhuskers** (p. 164) — After three likely nonconference wins at home, Nebraska’s schedule picks up in October, having to take on playoff teams in consecutive weeks, hosting Indiana and traveling to Oregon.

- **Northwestern Wildcats** (p. 166) — That excitement gets a dose of reality though when you look at the Wildcats’ schedule.

- **Indiana Hoosiers** (p. 152) — Unfortunately for Cignetti’s program, there is already a famous movie titled “Hoosiers” because last season is certainly worthy of having its story told in a film as the longtime doormat of the Big Ten became a college football powerhouse.
